definitions.formula: \forall Y\in\mathbf V'\subseteq\mathbf V:\quad\Pr(Y\mid\operatorname{Pa}_Y;\theta_Y)\longmapsto I(Y\mid\operatorname{Pa}^*_Y;\theta_Y^*).
definitions.assumptions: SCG mechanisms and replacement CPDs; interventions preserve Markov compatibility and the causal graph's admissible structure.
definitions.gloss: Replace selected variable mechanisms to ask how behaviour or outcomes would change.
definitions.relation: Ordinary intervention specialized by Context-Conditional Intervention; used in belief and intention tests.

definitions.quote: An agent i responds [29] to a proposition ϕ if they act differently when they observe that ϕ is i true to when they observe that ϕ is false,
definitions.formula: D^i_{\phi=\bot}(\pi_{i(\phi)},\mathbf e)\ne D^i_{\phi=\top}(\pi_{i(\phi)},\mathbf e).
definitions.assumptions: Single-decision SCG; access to the unique observation-conditioned policy; intervene on the observation, not the proposition; proposition contains no decision descendants.
definitions.gloss: The agent changes its decision when told the proposition is true versus false.
definitions.relation: Prerequisite for Belief and Ignorance; differs from intervention on an underlying variable in Hammond et al.'s response incentive.

definitions.quote: Then, in words, for a proposition ϕ to which i responds, i believes ϕ if they act as though they observe ϕ is true.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{Bel}_i(\phi;\pi,\mathbf e)\iff \bigl[D^i_{\phi=\bot}(\pi_{i(\phi)},\mathbf e)\ne D^i_{\phi=\top}(\pi_{i(\phi)},\mathbf e)\bigr]\land\bigl[D^i(\pi,\mathbf e)=D^i_{\phi=\top}(\pi_{i(\phi)},\mathbf e)\bigr].
definitions.assumptions: As for response; policy profile and exogenous setting fixed. This operationalizes acceptance; nonresponse makes belief unidentifiable.
definitions.gloss: A responsive agent believes a proposition when its actual action matches its action after observing that proposition as true.
definitions.relation: Used by Deception and Ignorance; alternative to mental-state or credence-based belief.

definitions.quote: An agent has a true belief about ϕ if they believe ϕ and ϕ is true (similarly for a false belief).
definitions.formula: \operatorname{TrueBel}_i(\phi)=\operatorname{Bel}_i(\phi)\land\phi;\qquad \operatorname{FalseBel}_i(\phi)=\operatorname{Bel}_i(\phi)\land\neg\phi.
definitions.assumptions: Belief as in Definition 3.1 and the actual truth value of the proposition in the SCG setting.
definitions.gloss: Classifies an accepted proposition by whether it is actually true.
definitions.relation: Specializations of Belief; false belief is required for Deception and lack of true belief defines Ignorance.

definitions.quote: First, we define a context-conditional intervention which only occurs in some settings.
definitions.formula: Y_{I\mid w}(\pi,\mathbf e)=\begin{cases}Y_I(\pi,\mathbf e)&\mathbf e\in w,\\Y(\pi,\mathbf e)&\mathbf e\notin w.\end{cases}
definitions.assumptions: An intervention I, SCG, policy profile, and specified subset w of exogenous settings.
definitions.gloss: Apply an intervention only in selected exogenous circumstances.
definitions.relation: Restricts an ordinary intervention to selected settings; used by Intention and renamed Contextual Intervention in Ward et al. (2024).

definitions.quote: Informally, an agent intended to cause an outcome X = x with its policy, if guaranteeing that another policy would cause X = x would make that policy just as good for the agent.

definitions.gloss: The outcome helps explain choosing this policy: securing it under an alternative removes the alternative's disadvantage.
definitions.relation: Refines H&KW Intention to influence and replaces Intention to bring about; implies Actual causality; antecedent of Deception.

definitions.quote: Following Carson [15], Mahon [58], we say that an agent S deceives another agent T if S intentionally causes T to believe ϕ, where ϕ is false and S does not believe that ϕ is true.

definitions.gloss: A responsive agent lacks a true belief about the proposition.

definitions.gloss: The agent prefers its policy because of its effects on a minimal collection of variables.
definitions.relation: Adaptation of Halpern–Kleiman-Weiner; variable-level precursor to Intention and prerequisite of Intention to bring about.

definitions.quote: In words, an agent i intends to bring about X = x with policy π i if 1) agent i intends to influence X with π i , 2) X = x is a possible outcome under π, 3) X = x is an optimal outcome for i under π.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{Influence}_i(\mathbf X;\pi^i,\hat\pi^i)\ \land\ \Pr_\pi(\mathbf X=\mathbf x)>0\ \land\ \forall\mathbf x'\in\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf X)\text{ with }\Pr_\pi(\mathbf X=\mathbf x')>0:\ \sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E_\pi[U_{\mathbf X=\mathbf x'}]\le\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E_\pi[U_{\mathbf X=\mathbf x}].

definitions.gloss: Among possible outcomes of an intentionally influenced variable, identifies utility-maximizing outcomes as intended.

definitions.quote: An intervention is a new set of structural functions I over a set of variables 𝒀 ⊆ 𝑽 that replaces the structural function 𝑓 𝑌 with a new function I𝑌 for each 𝑌 ∈ 𝒀 , which may have a different domain, i.e., may change the parents of the variables in 𝒀 .

definitions.gloss: Replace selected causal functions, possibly changing their parent variables.
definitions.relation: General intervention on which Contextual Intervention and the two formal intention definitions are based.

definitions.quote: An agent intended to cause an outcome 𝑜 with its action 𝑎, if guaranteeing that another action 𝑎 ′ also caused 𝑜 would make 𝑎 ′ just as good for the agent.
definitions.assumptions: Comparison with an alternative action; a meaningful operation that guarantees the outcome; an ordering of actions by desirability.
definitions.gloss: An outcome is intended if guaranteeing it would make another action equally good.
definitions.relation: First approximation refined by Operationalisations II and III and formalized by Subjective Intention.

definitions.quote: An agent intended to cause outcomes 𝒐 with action 𝑎, if there exists a super-set of outcomes 𝒚 ⊇ 𝒐 such that guaranteeing another action 𝑎 ′ also caused 𝒚 would make 𝑎 ′ just as good, and no proper subset of 𝒚 makes 𝑎 ′ as good as 𝑎.
definitions.assumptions: Alternative action and counterfactual guarantees for collections of outcomes; subset-minimality.
definitions.gloss: An outcome can be one of several jointly sufficient reasons for acting, excluding unnecessary side effects.
definitions.relation: Generalizes Operationalisation I to multiple outcomes; refined by Operationalisation III.

definitions.quote: An agent intended to cause outcomes 𝒐 in setting 𝒆 with action 𝑎, if (1) There is a super-set of outcomes 𝒚 ⊇ 𝒐 and a set of settings 𝒘 ⊇ 𝒆 in which 𝒚 is caused; (2) Guaranteeing that another action 𝑎 ′ also caused 𝒚 in 𝒘 would make 𝑎 ′ just as good as 𝑎; (3) No proper subsets of 𝒚 and 𝒘 make 𝑎 ′ just as good as 𝑎.
definitions.assumptions: Random settings, alternative action, and counterfactual guarantees restricted to selected settings; minimal outcome and setting sets.
definitions.gloss: Only outcomes in circumstances essential to the reason for acting count as intended.
definitions.relation: Refines Operationalisation II by excluding coincidental outcomes; formalized by Subjective Intention.

definitions.quote: First, we define a contextual intervention which only occurs in some exogenous settings.
definitions.formula: I^Y_{\mathbf w_Y}(\mathbf{pa}_Y,\mathbf e)=\begin{cases}I^Y(\mathbf{pa}_Y)&\mathbf e\in\mathbf w_Y,\\f^Y(\mathbf{pa}_Y)&\mathbf e\notin\mathbf w_Y,\end{cases}\qquad I^Y_{\mathbf w_Y}:\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf{Pa}_Y\cup\mathbf E)\to\operatorname{dom}(Y).
definitions.assumptions: SCIM structural functions and selected exogenous settings. The intervened function may depend on every exogenous variable and make the model non-Markovian.
definitions.gloss: Apply a replacement mechanism only in chosen exogenous circumstances.
definitions.relation: Same construction as Context-Conditional Intervention in Ward et al. (2023); supports Subjective and Behavioural Intention.

definitions.quote: The agent intentionally causes the outcomes of 𝑶 in setting 𝒆 with 𝜋 if the following conditions are met.
definitions.formula: \exists\mathbf Y\supseteq\mathbf O,\ W=\{\mathbf w_Y\}_{Y\in\mathbf Y},\ \hat\pi\in\operatorname{REF}(\pi):\quad \mathbf w_Y\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf E),\quad \mathbf e\in\bigcap_{O\in\mathbf O}\mathbf w_O,\quad \mathbb E_\pi\!\left[\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}U\right]\le\mathbb E_{\hat\pi}\!\left[\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}U_{\mathbf Y_\pi\mid W}\right],\quad\mathbf Y\text{ and each }\mathbf w_Y\text{ subset-minimal}.
definitions.assumptions: Single-decision subjective SCIM, utility function, actual policy and reference alternatives; contextual interventions. Model need not match reality.
definitions.gloss: An intended outcome belongs to a minimal collection of effects that justify the policy over an alternative.
definitions.relation: Formalizes Operationalisation III; refines H&KW Intention to influence/bring about; equivalent to Behavioural Intention under Theorem 14's conditions.

definitions.quote: Following this, we represent an adaptive agent as a policy oracle which maps interventions in a SCIM to policies [32].
definitions.formula: \Gamma:\mathcal I_M\to\Pi_M;\qquad \Gamma\text{ robustly optimal}\iff\forall I\in\mathcal I_M,\ \Gamma(I)\in\arg\max_\pi\mathbb E^{M_I}_\pi\!\left[\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}U\right].

definitions.gloss: Represents how an agent chooses policies as its environment changes; robust optimality requires utility maximization under every intervention.
definitions.relation: Agent representation used by Behavioural Intention; robust optimality helps equate it to Subjective Intention.

definitions.quote: The following definition is similar to Definition 6, except that we replace condition 2) with a requirement that the agent should observably change its behaviour when the intended outcomes are fixed.
definitions.formula: \pi:=\Gamma(M),\quad \exists\mathbf Y\supseteq\mathbf O,\ W=\{\mathbf w_Y\}_{Y\in\mathbf Y}:\ \mathbf e\in\bigcap_{O\in\mathbf O}\mathbf w_O,\quad \Gamma(M)\ne\Gamma(M_{\mathbf Y_\pi\mid W}),\quad \mathbf Y\text{ and every }\mathbf w_Y\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf E)\text{ subset-minimal}.
definitions.assumptions: Intervention access and policy oracle; no utility variables required. Interpretation as subjective intent requires robust optimality, stable causal representation, and Theorem 14's tie-breaking assumption.
definitions.gloss: If guaranteeing selected outcomes changes the agent's policy, those outcomes reveal its reasons for acting.
definitions.relation: Behavioural counterpart of Subjective Intention; equivalent under robust optimality and specified preference for the baseline policy on ties.

definitions.quote: Condition (2) does most of the work. It is a necessity condition capturing the “but-for" clause, that is, but for the fact that 𝑪 = 𝒄 occurred, 𝑶 = 𝒐 would not have occurred.
definitions.formula: \mathbf C_\pi(\mathbf e)=\mathbf c,\quad\mathbf O_\pi(\mathbf e)=\mathbf o;\qquad\exists\mathbf Z\subseteq\mathbf V,\ \mathbf c'\in\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf C):\ \mathbf z=\mathbf Z_\pi(\mathbf e),\quad\mathbf O_{\mathbf C=\mathbf c',\mathbf Z=\mathbf z,\pi}(\mathbf e)\ne\mathbf o;\qquad\mathbf C\text{ subset-minimal}.
definitions.assumptions: SCIM, policy and exogenous setting; interventions holding contingency variables at actual values. PDF Definition 15 prints the final comparison as ≠ O rather than ≠ o; formula makes the outcome comparison explicit.
definitions.gloss: A minimal actual event whose alteration changes the outcome under a suitable actual-valued contingency.
definitions.relation: Adaptation of Halpern's actual causality; implied by Subjective Intention in the subjective model (Theorem 7).

definitions.quote: In a SCIM M there is an ICI on 𝑂 if for all optimal 𝜋 ∗ there exists 𝑑 ∈ 𝑑𝑜𝑚(𝐷) s.t.
definitions.formula: \forall\pi^*\in\operatorname{Opt}(M)\ \exists d\in\operatorname{dom}(D):\quad\mathbb E_{\pi^*}\!\left[\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}U\right]\ne\mathbb E_{\pi^*}\!\left[\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}U_{O_{D=d}}\right].

definitions.quote: The simplest form of intervention, a hard intervention do(Y = y), sets the values of variables Y to some y.
definitions.formula: \Pr_{\mathbf y}(v\mid\mathbf{pa}_V)=\begin{cases}1&V\in\mathbf Y,\ v\text{ consistent with }\mathbf y,\\\Pr(v\mid\mathbf{pa}_V)&V\notin\mathbf Y,\ \mathbf{pa}_V\text{ consistent with }\mathbf y.\end{cases}
definitions.assumptions: Causal Bayesian network and variables to fix; inconsistent variable assignments have probability zero; conditioning on impossible parent assignments is undefined.
definitions.gloss: Force selected variables to specified values, leaving other mechanisms unchanged.
definitions.relation: Special case of Soft intervention; the action step of counterfactual evaluation.

definitions.quote: More generally, a soft intervention, specified using a partial distribution I over variables Y replaces each CPD Pr(Y | PaY ) with a new CPD I(Y | Pa∗Y ; θY∗ ) for each Y ∈ Y , where Pa∗Y may differ from PaY .3
definitions.formula: \Pr_I(\mathbf v):=\prod_{Y\in\mathbf Y}I(y\mid\mathbf{pa}^*_Y)\prod_{V\in\mathbf V\setminus\mathbf Y}\Pr(v\mid\mathbf{pa}_V).
definitions.assumptions: Known causal graph and mechanisms; replacement CPDs and potentially changed parents. SCG interventions require deterministic mechanisms with any fresh randomness made exogenous.
definitions.gloss: Replace selected mechanisms, possibly changing what inputs they depend on.
definitions.relation: Generalizes Hard intervention; used in interventional and counterfactual queries.

definitions.quote: In counterfactual queries, evidence about the actual state of the world informs us about a hypothetical scenario in which some variables have been modified.
definitions.formula: \Pr(\mathbf x_I\mid\mathbf z)=\int_{\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf E)}\Pr_I(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf e)\Pr(\mathbf e\mid\mathbf z)\,d\mathbf e.
definitions.assumptions: Markovian SCM with independent exogenous noise and deterministic endogenous functions; observation has positive probability. Formula expresses the three steps in Definition 5's following discussion.
definitions.gloss: Update hidden circumstances from actual evidence, then evaluate a hypothetical intervention in those same circumstances.
definitions.relation: SCM precursor to Counterfactual query in games (Definition 23).

definitions.quote: In the definition below, we therefore consider the distribution Prπ (x | z) induced by each rational outcome that is consistent with the observation z.
definitions.formula: \Pr^R(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf z):=\{\Pr^\pi(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf z)\}_{\pi\in R(mM\mid\mathbf z)},\qquad R(mM\mid\mathbf z):=\{\pi\in R(mM):\Pr^\pi(\mathbf z)>0\}.
definitions.assumptions: Mechanised MAID, known rationality relations and parameters; enumerate all rational outcomes consistent with the observation, which may include mechanism variables.
definitions.gloss: Return predictions for every rational policy profile compatible with the evidence.
definitions.relation: Associational component reused in Interventional query and Counterfactual query in games.

definitions.quote: A causal game (CG) M = (G, θ) is a MAID such that for any parameterisation of the decision variable CPDs π, the induced model with joint distribution Prπ (V ) is a CBN.
definitions.formula: M=(G,\theta)\text{ is a CG}\iff\forall\pi,\ (G,\theta,\pi)\text{ induces a causal Bayesian network with distribution }\Pr^\pi(\mathbf V).
definitions.assumptions: MAID with decision, chance and utility variables; graph represents causal rather than merely statistical relationships.
definitions.gloss: A game whose causal interpretation remains valid after any choice of policies.
definitions.relation: Causal extension of MAIDs; generalized to counterfactual-capable Structural causal games.

definitions.quote: Our key observation is that pre-policy interventions can be modelled as interventions on the mechanism variables in the mechanised CG, which ensures that the effects are propagated through the processes via which agents select their decision rules.
definitions.assumptions: Mechanised CG; agents know pre-policy changes before selecting policies; post-policy changes occur without policy adaptation. Timing concerns available information, not chronological play.
definitions.gloss: Pre-policy changes let agents adapt their policies; post-policy changes act on the world with those policies fixed.
definitions.relation: Two cases of Interventional query and Counterfactual query in games; encoded at mechanism and object levels, respectively.

definitions.quote: As for conditional queries, in our definition (which mirrors that introduced for cyclic causal models [8], but where the cyclic dependencies are governed by relations instead of functions [1]) we quantify over the set of rational outcomes that are consistent with the given intervention.
definitions.formula: \Pr^R(\mathbf x_I):=\{\Pr^\pi(\mathbf x_I)\}_{\pi\in R(mM_I)},\qquad R^*=\{r_D^*\}_{\Pi_D\in\mathbf Y}\cup\{r_D\}_{\Pi_D\notin\mathbf Y}.
definitions.assumptions: Mechanised CG, rationality relations and intervention on object-level or mechanism variables; resulting parameter distributions and rational responses determine R(mM_I).
definitions.gloss: Return the intervention's consequences under all rational outcomes of the changed game.
definitions.relation: Generalizes causal-model interventions to adaptive agents; observation-free counterpart of Counterfactual query in games.

definitions.quote: An SCG can be seen as an SCM without parameters for the decision variables.
definitions.formula: M=(G,\theta)\text{ is a Markovian SCG}\iff\forall\dot\pi,\ \Pr^{\dot\pi}(\mathbf V,\mathbf E)\text{ is induced by a Markovian SCM}.
definitions.assumptions: A causal game with exogenous and endogenous variables; one independent exogenous parent per endogenous variable; deterministic CPDs after selecting deterministic decision rules.
definitions.gloss: Add explicit exogenous randomness so that fixing deterministic policies yields a structural causal model.
definitions.relation: Extends Causal game to counterfactuals; subsumes SCMs and single-agent SCIMs.

definitions.quote: Given a stochastic decision rule πD (D | PaD ), we may then define a canonical structural representation by setting:
definitions.formula: \Pr(E_D^{\pi_D,\mathbf{pa}_D}=d):=\pi_D(d\mid\mathbf{pa}_D),\qquad\dot\pi_D(D=d\mid\mathbf{pa}_D,\mathbf e_D):=\delta_{D,e_D^{\pi_D,\mathbf{pa}_D}},\qquad \mathbf{Pa}_D:=\operatorname{Pa}_D\setminus\{E_D\}.
definitions.assumptions: Stochastic behavioural decision rules; independent randomization across different rules and non-exogenous decision contexts; random-field exogenous variables held fixed across worlds.
definitions.where: §4.3, Decision Rules as Structural Functions, equation (3), [P258]–[P264]
definitions.gloss: Realize each stochastic choice using a separate exogenous draw indexed by policy and decision context.
definitions.relation: Makes stochastic policies usable in Structural causal games; a modeling assumption needed for Counterfactual query in games.

definitions.quote: The simplest – let us call it the simplicity principle – is to recompute the values of all decision rule variables, i.e., Π(I) = ∅.
definitions.formula: \Pi(I)=\varnothing\quad\text{for pre-policy counterfactuals};\qquad\Pi(I)=\Pi\quad\text{for fully post-policy interventions}.
definitions.assumptions: An SCG with possibly multiple rational outcomes; pre-policy intervention; do not assume preservation of actual-world equilibrium choices.
definitions.gloss: Recompute all policy choices after a pre-policy intervention.
definitions.relation: Alternative to Closest possible world principle; supplies invariance set for Definition 23.

definitions.quote: When computing counterfactuals in SCGs under the ‘closest possible world’ principle, our basic desideratum is to consider those counterfactual rational outcomes π 0 ∈ R(mMI ) that are consistent with the decision rules used in some actual rational outcome π ∈ R(mM | z) whenever those decision rules are not affected by I.
definitions.assumptions: Mechanised SCG, actual evidence, intervention, and R-relevance graph. Appendix B.1 Algorithm 1 propagates changes through maximal strongly connected components, retaining components whose rational-response sets remain unchanged.
definitions.gloss: Preserve actual-world policy information wherever the intervention leaves rational choices unaffected.
definitions.relation: Alternative to Simplicity principle; produces a larger invariant-policy set for Counterfactual query in games.

definitions.quote: Given a set of invariant decision rule variables Π(I), the answer produced by the three-step process given above can be written as follows.
definitions.formula: \Pr^R(\mathbf x_I\mid\mathbf z):=\left\{\int_{\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf E')}\Pr^{\pi'}(\mathbf x_I\mid\mathbf e,\mathbf e^*)\Pr(\mathbf e^*)\Pr^\pi(\mathbf e\mid\mathbf z)\,d\mathbf e'\right\}_{(\pi,\pi')\in R(mM_I\mid\mathbf z)},\quad R(mM_I\mid\mathbf z):=\{(\pi,\pi')\in R(mM\mid\mathbf z)\times R(mM_I):\pi(I)=\pi'(I)\}.
definitions.assumptions: Mechanised SCG, rationality relations, deterministic mechanisms or canonical structural policy representation, positive-probability observation, and an explicit invariance principle. E*=E'\E captures fresh independent intervention noise.
definitions.gloss: Combine actual evidence with hypothetical changes, returning every compatible actual/counterfactual policy pair's answer.
definitions.relation: Generalizes SCM counterfactuals to adaptive multi-agent games; contains pre- and post-policy cases; depends on the chosen invariance principle.

definitions.quote: The following definition is adapted from [39], and formalises the extent to which an agent is blameworthy for causing an event.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{db}_S(d,d',\phi):=\delta_{d,d',\phi}\frac{S-\max(c^i(d')-c^i(d),0)}{S},\quad\delta_{d,d',\phi}:=\max(0,\Pr^\pi(\phi_d)-\Pr^\pi(\phi_{d'})),\quad c^i(d):=\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E^\pi[U]-\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E^\pi[U_d],\quad S>\max_d c^i(d),\quad\operatorname{db}_S(d,\phi):=\max_{d'}\operatorname{db}_S(d,d',\phi).
definitions.assumptions: Known SCG, policy profile, decision and alternatives, proposition, agent utilities, and cost-sensitivity S.
definitions.gloss: Blame increases with the decision's effect on an event's probability and decreases when avoiding it would have been costly.
definitions.relation: Adapts Halpern–Kleiman-Weiner blameworthiness to SCGs; distinct from actual causation and from Intention to bring about.

definitions.quote: In the same work as above, the authors also formalise the question of whether or not an agent intends to bring about an event, which we adapt below for use with SCGs.
definitions.formula: \exists\mathbf Z\supseteq\mathbf Y\text{ subset-minimal}:\ \sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E^\pi[U_d]\le\max_{d'\in\operatorname{alt}(d)}\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E^\pi[U_{d',\mathbf z_d}];\quad \Pr^\pi(\mathbf y_d)>0;\quad\forall\mathbf y'\in\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf Y)\text{ with }\Pr^\pi(\mathbf y'_d)>0:\ \sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E^\pi[U_{\mathbf y'}]\le\sum_{U\in\mathbf U^i}\mathbb E^\pi[U_{\mathbf y}].
definitions.assumptions: SCG with fixed policy profile, utilities, reference alternative decisions, and nested counterfactuals; game structure and prior are common knowledge.
definitions.gloss: Intended outcomes belong to minimally influential variables, are achievable, and maximize utility among the possible outcomes.
definitions.relation: Adapts H&KW action-level intention; related to Ward's policy-level Intention to influence and Intention to bring about.

definitions.quote: X has a response incentive (RI) if all optimal policies π ∗ respond to X, and a graph G admits a RI on X if there is a SCIM over G that has a RI on X.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{Respond}(\pi,X)\iff\exists x\in\operatorname{dom}(X),\mathbf e\in\operatorname{dom}(\mathbf E):\Pr^\pi(D_x\mid\mathbf e)\ne\Pr^\pi(D\mid\mathbf e);\qquad\operatorname{RI}_M(X)\iff\forall\pi^*\in\operatorname{Opt}(M),\operatorname{Respond}(\pi^*,X).
definitions.assumptions: Single-agent, single-decision SCIM; optimal policies and intervention access while fixing exogenous context; graph admission existentially quantifies over SCIM parameterizations.
definitions.gloss: Every optimal policy must sometimes change its decision when the variable is changed.
definitions.relation: Distinct from Ward's response to an observed proposition; complements Instrumental control incentive's influence-on-the-world criterion.

definitions.quote: In a single-decision SCIM M, there is an instrumental control incentive (ICI) on a variable X in decision context paD if for all optimal policies π ∗ , there exists some d ∈ dom(D) such that:
definitions.formula: \forall\pi^*\in\operatorname{Opt}(M)\ \exists d\in\operatorname{dom}(D):\quad\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}\mathbb E^{\pi^*}[U_{X_d}\mid\mathbf{pa}_D]\ne\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}\mathbb E^{\pi^*}[U\mid\mathbf{pa}_D].
definitions.assumptions: Single-agent, single-decision SCIM, utility and optimal policies, specified decision context, and nested counterfactual intervention through X. Graph admission means some parameterized SCIM has such an incentive.
definitions.gloss: Changing the decision's influence through this variable changes expected utility under every optimal policy.
definitions.relation: Context-specific version of the ICI reproduced in Ward et al. (2024); shares intention's decision-to-variable-to-utility graphical pattern.

definitions.quote: The local explanation for model f at instance x is some relevant property of x, denoted e(x). The selected property should ideally be enough, on its own, to predict label f (x).
definitions.formula: f:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y,\qquad e:\mathcal X\to\mathcal E,\qquad \text{local explanation at }x=e(x).
definitions.assumptions: Classifier and explanation function; randomized explainers may be fixed to one seed. Explanations are properties, not necessarily subsets of raw features.
definitions.gloss: A property of an instance offered as sufficient information for predicting the model's label.
definitions.relation: Framework underlying consistency, sufficiency, and intelligibility.

definitions.quote: The consistency of explainer e for model f at instance x, with respect to distribution µ, is defined as
definitions.formula: C_\pi:=\{x\in\mathcal X:e(x)=\pi\},\quad\pi=e(x),\qquad m_c(x):=\Pr_{x'\sim\mu|C_\pi}\bigl(f(x')=f(x)\bigr).
definitions.assumptions: Classifier, explainer and deployment distribution; conditional sampling among instances receiving exactly the same explanation; conditional distribution must be defined.
definitions.gloss: How often another instance receiving this explanation has the same predicted label.
definitions.relation: One component of faithfulness; differs from Local sufficiency, which conditions on applicability rather than assignment.

definitions.quote: The global consistency of explanation system (f, e), with respect to distribution µ over X , is
definitions.formula: m_c:=\mathbb E_{x\sim\mu}[m_c(x)]=1-E_G.
definitions.assumptions: Classifier, explainer, deployment distribution, and defined local consistency almost surely.
definitions.gloss: Average label agreement among points assigned the same explanation; equivalently, Gibbs-decoder accuracy.
definitions.relation: Averages Local consistency; equals accuracy of the Gibbs decoder and bounds optimal deterministic decoding error.

definitions.quote: To start with, we say that explanations E are intelligible if for any instance x ∈ X and property π ∈ E, it is possible to assess whether π applies to x.
definitions.formula: A:\mathcal X\times\mathcal E\to\{0,1\},\qquad C_x:=\{x'\in\mathcal X:A(x',e(x))\}.
definitions.assumptions: An applicability relation based solely on the instance and explanation, independent of true or predicted label. Human checkability is desirable but not required by the definition.
definitions.gloss: One can decide whether an explanation's property holds for an instance.
definitions.relation: Required to define Local sufficiency; explicitly scoped rules supply a direct applicability relation.

definitions.quote: The local sufficiency of explainer e for model f at instance x, with respect to distribution µ, is defined as
definitions.formula: C_x:=\{x'\in\mathcal X:A(x',e(x))\},\qquad m_s(x):=\Pr_{x'\sim\mu|C_x}\bigl(f(x')=f(x)\bigr).
definitions.assumptions: Classifier, explainer, intelligible applicability relation, and deployment distribution; defined conditional distribution over applicable instances.
definitions.gloss: How often another instance satisfying the stated property has the same predicted label.
definitions.relation: Complementary to Local consistency; equals anchor precision for anchor explanations.

definitions.quote: The global sufficiency of explanation system (f, e), with respect to distribution µ on X , is equal to ms = Ex∈µ X [ms (x)].
definitions.formula: m_s:=\mathbb E_{x\sim\mu}[m_s(x)].
definitions.assumptions: Classifier, explainer, deployment distribution and applicability relation; local sufficiency defined almost surely.
definitions.gloss: Average sufficiency of the explanations issued on the deployment distribution.
definitions.relation: Averages Local sufficiency; equals average anchor precision; need not exceed or fall below Global consistency.

definitions.quote: With this in place, there are two natural ways to define the decoder: (i) the (randomized) Gibbs decoder that, given explanation π, returns a label y with probability Pr(y|π), and (ii) the optimal deterministic decoder that returns the label y that maximizes Pr(y|π).
definitions.formula: p(y\mid\pi):=\Pr_{x\sim\mu|C_\pi}(f(x)=y),\quad d_G(\pi)\sim p(\cdot\mid\pi),\quad d_O(\pi)\in\arg\max_y p(y\mid\pi),\quad E_d:=\Pr_x(f(x)\ne d(e(x))),\quad E_O\le E_G\le2E_O.
definitions.assumptions: Distribution of predicted labels conditional on explanation; unrestricted optimal decoder, not a bounded human or learned simulator.
definitions.where: §2.1, Relation to decoding and Claim 1, [P37]–[P40]; Appendix A.1 [P166]
definitions.gloss: Recover the model's label from its explanation by conditional sampling or by the most likely label.
definitions.relation: Global consistency is exactly Gibbs-decoder accuracy; optimal deterministic decoding is within a factor of two in error.

definitions.quote: The quality of an anchor is typically formalized using the notion of precision, which is the probability, over the distribution µ, that a random instance in Hx has label f (x), that is, Prx0 ∈µ Hx [f (x0 ) = f (x)].
definitions.formula: \operatorname{precision}(H_x):=\Pr_{x'\sim\mu|H_x}[f(x')=f(x)].
definitions.assumptions: Explicit hyperrectangle H_x containing x, classifier, and deployment distribution; conditional distribution on H_x exists.
definitions.gloss: Agreement with the target label among points inside the anchor region.
definitions.relation: Special case of Local sufficiency; mean precision equals Global sufficiency.

definitions.quote: To formalize it, we say an explanation system (f, e) has explicitly scoped rules if each explanation π is a description of a region Sπ ⊆ X of the instance space. For a given point x, the explanation π = e(x) has the property that x ∈ Sπ . The terminology “explicitly scoped” means that subset Sπ is specified in a form where it is easy to check whether a specific point lies in it or not.
definitions.formula: \pi=e(x)\implies x\in S_\pi\subseteq\mathcal X,\qquad A(x,\pi)\iff x\in S_\pi.
definitions.assumptions: Explanation supplies an explicit region with easy membership checks and contains its explained instance.
definitions.gloss: Each explanation declares a region of inputs, and membership can be checked directly.
definitions.relation: A subclass of Intelligible explanations; includes decision-tree paths, anchors, and highlighted text.

definitions.quote: In this case, the “explanation” x0 gives information about the nature of predictions in the vicinity of x. Specifically, it asserts that any point in the open ball B(x, d(x, x0 )) has label f (x).
definitions.formula: x'\in\arg\min_{z:f(z)\ne f(x)}d(x,z).
definitions.assumptions: Classifier, input metric, and existence of a nearest oppositely classified instance; closest-point formulation specializes to binary classification.
definitions.gloss: A nearby input with a different model prediction, concretized as the nearest such input.
definitions.relation: Can be converted to an explicitly scoped open-ball rule and assessed using sufficiency; unlike SCM counterfactuals, no causal mechanism is required.

definitions.quote: This generalizes both types of faithfulness: for consistency, take R(x, π) to mean e(x) = π and for sufficiency take R(x, π) ≡ A(x, π).
definitions.formula: m_\mu^R:=\Pr_{X,X'\sim\mu}\bigl(f(X')=f(X)\mid R(X',e(X))\bigr).
definitions.assumptions: Classifier, explainer, relation R and deployment distribution. This is the main-text printed formula; Appendix A.2 instead writes E_X[q(f(X)|e(X))], matching the intended average of local conditional scores. The two sampling orders are not generally identical.
definitions.gloss: Use one relation-based agreement criterion to express both consistency and sufficiency.
definitions.relation: Generalizes the two faithfulness components; target of the global estimator, subject to the printed conditioning ambiguity.

definitions.quote: Our estimator for mR µ is then
definitions.formula: \widehat M:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{N_{e(x_i)}>1\}\frac{N_{e(x_i),f(x_i)}-1}{N_{e(x_i)}-1},\quad N_\pi:=|\{i:R(x_i,\pi)\}|,\quad N_{\pi,y}:=|\{i:R(x_i,\pi),f(x_i)=y\}|.
definitions.assumptions: Independent unlabeled samples from the deployment distribution plus queries to f and e; countable explanation space; computable R with self-applicability. Terms with no other matching point contribute zero.
definitions.gloss: Average leave-one-out label agreement among examples sharing an explanation or satisfying its property.
definitions.relation: Estimates the average local version of Generic faithfulness; specializes to Global consistency or Global sufficiency.

definitions.quote: To estimate consistency it returns the fraction of instances with similar label out of all instances with similar explanation. To estimate sufficiency, it returns the fraction of instances with similar label out of all examples that e(x) applied to.
definitions.formula: \widehat m_c(x)=\frac{\sum_{x'\in S}\mathbf1\{e(x')=e(x),\,f(x')=f(x)\}}{\sum_{x'\in S}\mathbf1\{e(x')=e(x)\}},\qquad \widehat m_s(x)=\frac{\sum_{x'\in S}\mathbf1\{A(x',e(x)),\,f(x')=f(x)\}}{\sum_{x'\in S}\mathbf1\{A(x',e(x))\}}.
definitions.assumptions: Sample S from µ and positive denominators. These are the fractions specified in the prose and counters; the PDF algorithm's last line mistakenly returns sufcounter/sufcounter rather than sufcounter/suftot.
definitions.gloss: Estimate each local score by the matching-label fraction among its relevant sampled inputs.
definitions.relation: Empirical counterparts of Local consistency and Local sufficiency; conditional sampling gives the stated Hoeffding sample bound.

definitions.quote: We also recorded the uniqueness of each explainer, which is the fraction of test data whose explanations were unique.
definitions.assumptions: Finite test sample, explanation equality, and predictions/explanations available. Measures repeatability relevant to estimation, not truth of the explanation itself.
definitions.gloss: The fraction of test examples whose explanations occur only once.
definitions.relation: Diagnoses missing repetition that makes the consistency/sufficiency estimators uninformative.

definitions.quote: Let ϕ represent a propositional formula, and let τA,B represent a term.
definitions.formula: \tau_{A,B}\models\phi,\qquad\forall\tau_{C,D}:\ (\tau_{A,B}\models\tau_{C,D}\land\tau_{A,B}\not\equiv\tau_{C,D})\implies\tau_{C,D}\not\models\phi.
definitions.assumptions: Propositional formula and consistent conjunctions of literals; a weaker term deletes literals. The first condition alone defines an implicant.
definitions.gloss: A sufficient conjunction of facts from which no literal can be removed without losing sufficiency.
definitions.relation: Logical basis of Abductive explanations and Global abductive explanations; distinct from Prime implicate.

definitions.quote: For completeness, we also mention prime implicates. Let ϕ be a propositional formula, and let ωA,B be a clause.
definitions.formula: \phi\models\omega_{A,B},\qquad\forall\omega_{C,D}:\ (\omega_{C,D}\models\omega_{A,B}\land\omega_{A,B}\not\equiv\omega_{C,D})\implies\phi\not\models\omega_{C,D}.
definitions.assumptions: Propositional formula and clauses. PDF condition 2 ends with τ_C,D rather than ω_C,D, an apparent symbol typo; formula states the clause-minimality condition described by the definition.
definitions.gloss: A necessary clause implied by the formula that cannot be strengthened by removing a literal.
definitions.relation: Dual to Prime implicant through minimal hitting sets; negated prime implicates define Counterexamples, not local Contrastive explanations.

definitions.quote: H is a minimal hitting set of S, if H is a hitting set of S, and there is no proper subset of H that is also a hitting set of S.
definitions.formula: \forall S_i\in\mathcal S,\ H\cap S_i\ne\varnothing,\qquad\forall H'\subsetneq H,\ \exists S_i\in\mathcal S:\ H'\cap S_i=\varnothing.
definitions.assumptions: A finite family of sets; subset minimality rather than minimum cardinality.
definitions.gloss: Touch every set using an irreducible collection of elements.
definitions.relation: Links MUSes with MCSes, prime implicants with prime implicates, and AXp's with CXp's.

definitions.quote: Informally, an MUS provides some irreducible information that suffices to be added to the background knowledge B to attain an inconsistent formula; thus, an MUS represents an explanation for the causes of inconsistency.
definitions.formula: \phi=\mathcal B\cup\mathcal S\models\bot,\quad\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal S,\quad\mathcal B\cup\mathcal M\models\bot,\quad\forall\mathcal M'\subsetneq\mathcal M,\ \mathcal B\cup\mathcal M'\not\models\bot.
definitions.assumptions: Consistent hard background constraints B; removable soft constraints S with B∪S inconsistent; sound and complete satisfiability reasoning.
definitions.gloss: An irreducible subset of soft constraints that conflicts with the fixed background.
definitions.relation: AXp computation reduces to MUS extraction; MUSes are minimal hitting sets of MCSes.

definitions.quote: Alternatively, one might be interested in correcting the formula, removing some clauses to achieve consistency.
definitions.formula: \mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S,\quad\mathcal B\cup(\mathcal S\setminus\mathcal C)\not\models\bot,\quad\forall\mathcal C'\subsetneq\mathcal C,\ \mathcal B\cup(\mathcal S\setminus\mathcal C')\models\bot.
definitions.assumptions: Hard background B and removable soft constraints S forming an inconsistent theory.
definitions.gloss: An irreducible set of constraints whose removal makes the theory consistent.
definitions.relation: CXp computation reduces to MCS extraction; dual to MUSes and complementary to MSSes.

definitions.quote: With each MCS C, one associates a Maximal Satisfiable Subset (MSS), given by S \ C.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{MSS}=\mathcal S\setminus\mathcal C\quad\text{for an MCS }\mathcal C.
definitions.assumptions: Same hard/soft partition as MCS; maximality is relative to soft constraints and fixed background.
definitions.gloss: A largest-by-inclusion compatible remainder after a minimal correction.
definitions.relation: Complement of an MCS; used in the optimization and explanation-computation discussion.

definitions.quote: Logic-based abduction can be viewed as the problem of finding a (minimimum or minimal) subset of hypotheses, which is consistent with some background theory, and such that those hypotheses are sufficient for some manifestation.
definitions.formula: \mathcal E\subseteq\mathcal H,\qquad\mathcal T\land\mathcal E\models\mathcal M,\qquad\mathcal T\land\mathcal E\not\models\bot.
definitions.assumptions: PAP=(X,H,M,T,ς): finite atoms, hypothesis clauses, manifestations, background theory, and nonnegative hypothesis costs. Minimum-cost or subset-minimal solutions may additionally be requested.
definitions.gloss: A consistent collection of hypotheses that entails the observations to be explained.
definitions.relation: General abduction framework instantiated by AXp's; prime-implicant computation is also an abduction instance.

definitions.quote: First, we mostly study a given local explanation problem EL = (M, v, c), with v ∈ F, c ∈ K and c = κ(v), which respects a concrete point in feature space, i.e. a concrete prediction. Second, we will also consider a global explanation problem EG = (M, c), with c ∈ K, which respects solely a concrete prediction c, that can be predicted in many points of feature space.
definitions.formula: E_L=(M,\mathbf v,c),\quad c=\kappa(\mathbf v);\qquad E_G=(M,c).
definitions.assumptions: Classifier M=(F,D,ℱ,K,κ), finite class set, feature domains, and either a particular classified instance or a target class.
definitions.gloss: Local problems explain one instance; global problems characterize a class across the feature space.
definitions.relation: Defines the domains of local AXp/CXp versus Global AXp/Counterexample.

definitions.quote: Thus, given an instance (v, c), a (weak) AXp is a subset of features which, if fixed to the values dictated by v, then the prediction is guaranteed to be c, independently of the values assigned to the other features.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{WeakAXp}(X):=\forall\mathbf x\in\mathbb F,\ \left[\bigwedge_{i\in X}(x_i=v_i)\right]\to(\kappa(\mathbf x)=c).
definitions.assumptions: Known classifier, target instance with c=κ(v), and feature space; all unselected-feature combinations are allowed unless input constraints are explicitly added.
definitions.gloss: Fixing the selected features guarantees the original prediction for every completion of the remaining features.
definitions.relation: Sufficiency criterion underlying AXp; generalized by WeakPAXp, input-constraint-aware AXp, and WeakLAXp.

definitions.quote: Moreover, X ⊆ F is an AXp if, besides being a weak AXp, it is also subsetminimal, i.e.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{AXp}(X):=\operatorname{WeakAXp}(X)\land\forall X'\subsetneq X,\neg\operatorname{WeakAXp}(X');\qquad\operatorname{AXp}(X)\iff\operatorname{WeakAXp}(X)\land\forall t\in X,\neg\operatorname{WeakAXp}(X\setminus\{t\}).
definitions.assumptions: Weak AXp setup; subset minimality, not necessarily smallest cardinality. Monotonicity makes checking single-feature deletions sufficient.
definitions.gloss: An irreducible set of feature values sufficient to guarantee the prediction.
definitions.relation: Boolean case equals PI-explanation; local prime implicant; minimal hitting-set dual of CXp; obtainable via MUS extraction.

definitions.quote: Thus, given an instance (v, c), a (weak) CXp is a subset of features which, if allowed to take any value from their domain, then there is an assignment to the features that changes the prediction to a class other than c, this while the features not in the explanation are kept to their values (ceteris paribus).
definitions.formula: \operatorname{WeakCXp}(Y):=\exists\mathbf x\in\mathbb F,\ \left[\bigwedge_{i\notin Y}(x_i=v_i)\right]\land(\kappa(\mathbf x)\ne c).
definitions.assumptions: Known classifier and target instance; selected features may vary over their domains, all other features fixed.
definitions.gloss: Changing only the selected features can produce a different prediction.
definitions.relation: Existential counterpart of Weak AXp and precursor to CXp; a feature-set counterfactual rather than an SCM intervention.

definitions.quote: Furthermore, a set Y ⊆ F is a CXp if, besides being a weak CXp, it is also subset-minimal, i.e.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{CXp}(Y):=\operatorname{WeakCXp}(Y)\land\forall Y'\subsetneq Y,\neg\operatorname{WeakCXp}(Y');\qquad\operatorname{CXp}(Y)\iff\operatorname{WeakCXp}(Y)\land\forall t\in Y,\neg\operatorname{WeakCXp}(Y\setminus\{t\}).
definitions.assumptions: Weak CXp setup and subset-minimality; monotonicity permits single-feature deletion tests.
definitions.gloss: An irreducible set of features that can be changed to change the prediction.
definitions.relation: Minimal hitting-set dual of AXp; reducible to MCS extraction; not a prime implicate or global Counterexample.

definitions.quote: The set of literals of π is a global abductive explanation of the prediction c.
definitions.formula: \pi\text{ is a prime implicant of }[\kappa(\mathbf x)=c],\qquad\forall\mathbf x\in\mathbb F,\ \pi(\mathbf x)\to(\kappa(\mathbf x)=c).
definitions.assumptions: Known classifier and target class; a consistent term of feature literals, irreducible under literal deletion; no fixed target instance.
definitions.gloss: A minimal sufficient rule guaranteeing a class across all inputs satisfying the rule.
definitions.relation: Global counterpart of AXp; corresponds to a prime implicant and is incompatible with every Counterexample for that class.

definitions.quote: The set of literals in η is referred to as a counterexample (CEx) for the prediction c, and represents the negation of a prime implicate for the predicate [κ(x) = c]. Clearly, both global AXp’s and CEx’s are irreducible (and so subset-minimal).
definitions.formula: \neg\eta\text{ is a prime implicate of }[\kappa(\mathbf x)=c];\qquad\forall\mathbf x\in\mathbb F,\ \eta(\mathbf x)\to(\kappa(\mathbf v)\ne c).
definitions.assumptions: Classifier and target class; η is a term. Displayed formula preserves the PDF's κ(v); its prose and prime-implicate definition instead require κ(x), an apparent variable typo.
definitions.gloss: A minimal conjunction ruling out the target class, expressed as a negated prime implicate.
definitions.relation: Global, class-level alternative to local CXp; every CEx breaks every Global AXp.

definitions.quote: Given the definition of (global) AXp’s and CEx’s (see Section 3.3), we say that two sets of literals break each other if these have inconsistent literals.
definitions.assumptions: Two sets of feature literals, with inconsistency determined by their feature-domain semantics.
definitions.where: §3.4, Duality between global AXp's and counterexamples, [P460]
definitions.gloss: The two literal sets cannot both hold because some literals conflict.
definitions.relation: Relation connecting every Global AXp with every CEx; distinct from local AXp/CXp hitting-set duality.

definitions.quote: A conflict set is a (subset)-minimal set CS of Comp such that,
definitions.formula: \mathrm{SD}\cup\{\neg\mathrm{Ab}(C_i):C_i\in\mathrm{CS}\}\cup\mathrm{Obs}\models\bot,\qquad\mathrm{CS}\text{ subset-minimal}.
definitions.assumptions: System description, components, abnormality predicate and observation; retaining assumptions that these components operate normally yields inconsistency.
definitions.gloss: A minimal collection of components whose normal-operation assumptions conflict with the observation.
definitions.relation: Model-based-diagnosis counterpart of MUS; the paper's classifier reduction maps minimal conflicts to AXp's.

definitions.quote: A diagnosis is a subset-minimal set ∆ of Comp such that,
definitions.formula: \mathrm{SD}\cup\{\neg\mathrm{Ab}(C_i):C_i\in\mathrm{Comp}\setminus\Delta\}\cup\mathrm{Obs}\not\models\bot,\qquad\Delta\text{ subset-minimal}.
definitions.assumptions: System description, components, abnormality predicate, observation, and a consistency checker.
definitions.gloss: A minimal set of components whose normal-operation assumptions must be relaxed to explain the observation consistently.
definitions.relation: Model-based-diagnosis counterpart of MCS; the paper's classifier reduction maps minimal diagnoses to CXp's.

definitions.quote: Second, for computing one AXp, the predicate to consider is:
definitions.formula: P_{\mathrm{axp}}(S;\mathcal T,F,\kappa,\mathbf v):=\neg\operatorname{CO}\!\left(\left\llbracket\left(\bigwedge_{i\in S}x_i=v_i\right)\land(\kappa(\mathbf x)\ne c)\right\rrbracket_{\mathcal T}\right).
definitions.assumptions: Faithful logic encoding of classifier and feature domains; sound, complete theory consistency oracle; c=κ(v).
definitions.gloss: Test whether fixing selected features makes a changed prediction impossible.
definitions.relation: Executable oracle criterion equivalent to Weak AXp; used by deletion-based AXp computation.

definitions.quote: and for computing one CXp, the predicate to consider is:
definitions.formula: P_{\mathrm{cxp}}(S;\mathcal T,F,\kappa,\mathbf v):=\operatorname{CO}\!\left(\left\llbracket\left(\bigwedge_{i\in F\setminus S}x_i=v_i\right)\land(\kappa(\mathbf x)\ne c)\right\rrbracket_{\mathcal T}\right).
definitions.assumptions: Faithful classifier encoding, feature domains, and sound, complete consistency oracle; c=κ(v).
definitions.gloss: Test whether changing only selected features permits a changed prediction.
definitions.relation: Executable criterion equivalent to Weak CXp; dual use of the same consistency oracle as Paxp.

definitions.quote: Given an explanation problem, and some set of already computed explanations (AXp’s and/or CXp’s), the query of enumeration of explainability is to find one explanation (AXp or CXp) among those that are not included in the set of explanations.
definitions.assumptions: Explanation problem and previously computed AXp/CXp set; completeness requires continuing until no unreported explanation remains.
definitions.gloss: Find another valid explanation outside those already returned.
definitions.relation: Uses AXp/CXp minimal hitting-set duality; extends computing just one explanation.

definitions.quote: The problem of deciding whether a given (possibly sensitive) feature is included in some explanation is referred to as the feature membership problem (FMP) [166].
definitions.formula: \exists X\subseteq F:\ t\in X\land\operatorname{AXp}(X),\qquad\text{equivalently }\exists Y\subseteq F:\ t\in Y\land\operatorname{CXp}(Y).
definitions.assumptions: Local explanation problem and target feature; access to classifier representation or relevant reasoning oracle.
definitions.gloss: Determine whether a feature appears in any minimal explanation of this prediction.
definitions.relation: Equivalent for AXp and CXp by duality; related to relevance in propositional abduction.

definitions.quote: A probabilistic (weak) AXp generalizes the definition of weak AXp, by allowing the prediction to change in some points of feature space, where a weak AXp would require the prediction not to change, but such that those changes have small probability.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{WeakPAXp}(X;\mathbb F,\kappa,\mathbf v,c,\delta):=\Pr_{\mathbf x}\bigl(\kappa(\mathbf x)=c\mid\mathbf x_X=\mathbf v_X\bigr)\ge\delta,\qquad0<\delta\le1.
definitions.assumptions: Known classifier and input distribution; finite categorical/ordinal feature domains and positive-probability conditioning event. Presented computations use uniform feature-space sampling; δ=1 recovers universal sufficiency under full support.
definitions.gloss: Fixing selected features makes the original label sufficiently likely rather than guaranteed.
definitions.relation: Probabilistic generalization of Weak AXp; also called a relevant set; basis for PAXp.

definitions.quote: Similarly to the deterministic case, a PAXp is a subset-minimal weak AXp.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{PAXp}(X):=\operatorname{WeakPAXp}(X)\land\forall X'\subsetneq X,\neg\operatorname{WeakPAXp}(X').
definitions.assumptions: WeakPAXp setup and threshold δ. Quoted sentence literally says 'weak AXp'; context refers to the probabilistic predicate in equation (28). Probabilistic sufficiency need not be monotone, so full subset-minimality matters.
definitions.gloss: An irreducible feature set meeting the probabilistic sufficiency threshold.
definitions.relation: Probabilistic counterpart of AXp; unlike universal AXp, checking only single-feature deletions does not generally prove minimality.

definitions.quote: For path Rk , the probability that a randomly chosen point in feature space is consistent with Rk (i.e. the path probability of Rk ) is given by,
definitions.formula: \Pr(R_k)=\frac{\left(\prod_{(x_i\in E_i)\in\Lambda(R_k)}|E_i|\right)\left(\prod_{i\in\Psi(R_k)}|D_i|\right)}{|\mathbb F|},\qquad\Pr_{\mathbf x}(\kappa(\mathbf x)=c\mid\mathbf x_X=\mathbf v_X)=\frac{\sum_{P_k\in\mathcal P}\#(P_k;\mathbf v,X)}{\sum_{R_k\in\mathcal R}\#(R_k;\mathbf v,X)},\quad\#(R_k;\mathbf v,X)=\prod_{i\in F}n_{ik}.
definitions.assumptions: Decision tree partitions feature space into disjoint consistent paths; finite domains and uniform input distribution. n_ik counts allowed feature values consistent with path k and any fixed feature values.
definitions.gloss: Count inputs consistent with tree paths to compute exact probabilities and test probabilistic explanations.
definitions.relation: Polynomial-time evaluation of WeakPAXp for decision trees; does not itself make finding minimal PAXp easy.

definitions.quote: Let us assume that a given classifier C is characterized by a constraint set IC capturing the allowed points in feature space.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{WeakAXp}_{IC}(X):=\forall\mathbf x\in\mathbb F,\ \left[\bigwedge_{i\in X}(x_i=v_i)\right]\to\left[IC(\mathbf x)\to(\kappa(\mathbf x)=c)\right];\qquad \operatorname{AXp}_{IC}(X)\iff\operatorname{WeakAXp}_{IC}(X)\land\forall X'\subsetneq X,\neg\operatorname{WeakAXp}_{IC}(X').
definitions.assumptions: Classifier, instance and known or learned valid-input predicate IC, normally with IC(v)=1; guarantees are relative to that constraint set.
definitions.gloss: Require the selected feature values to guarantee the prediction only on permitted inputs.
definitions.relation: Generalizes Weak AXp/AXp to restricted feature spaces; preserves AXp/CXp duality.

definitions.quote: Given the diverse nature of features, we opt to define the Hamming distance between two points in feature space,
definitions.formula: D_h(\mathbf x_1,\mathbf x_2)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\operatorname{ITE}(x_{1i}=x_{2i},1,0).
definitions.assumptions: Feature vectors of equal dimension. Formula is transcribed as printed: it counts equal coordinates, unlike standard Hamming distance, which counts unequal coordinates.
definitions.gloss: The printed expression counts matching coordinates, although the paper calls it Hamming distance.
definitions.relation: Locality predicate used in WeakLAXp and WeakLCXp; alternative distance measures are explicitly permitted.

definitions.quote: Given the definition of Hamming distance, we can now propose a definition of localized weak abductive and contrastive explanations.
definitions.formula: \operatorname{WeakLAXp}(X):=\forall\mathbf x\in\mathbb F,\ \left[D_h(\mathbf x,\mathbf v)\le\epsilon\land\bigwedge_{i\in X}(x_i=v_i)\right]\to(\kappa(\mathbf x)=c);\qquad\operatorname{LAXp}(X)\iff\operatorname{WeakLAXp}(X)\land\forall t\in X,\neg\operatorname{WeakLAXp}(X\setminus\{t\}).
definitions.assumptions: Classifier, instance, locality radius ε>0 and chosen distance. The printed D_h has the equality-counting issue noted under Hamming distance; the text permits other distance measures.
definitions.gloss: Selected features guarantee the prediction within a specified neighborhood; minimal versions remove unnecessary features.
definitions.relation: Locality-restricted Weak AXp/AXp; uses the same single-deletion minimality criterion.

definitions.assumptions: Classifier, instance and ε>0; a different-label witness in the neighborhood. The printed D_h counts equal coordinates; quoted replacement sentence repeats WeakAXp where its second occurrence evidently means WeakCXp.
definitions.gloss: Changing selected features can produce a nearby input with a different prediction; minimal versions remove unnecessary changes.
definitions.relation: Locality-restricted Weak CXp/CXp; counterpart to Localized abductive explanation.
